question: Avian atavism / evo-devo of reptilian ancestral traits in birds: what is genomically and developmentally mapped in birds (Aves), what ontogenetic programs they share with non-avian reptiles (Crocodylia, Squamata, Testudines), and what would have to be changed in silico to re-accentuate basal archosaur traits — specifically a long bony tail and mineralized teeth. Cover in depth: (1) Molecular basis of avian edentulism — pseudogenization of the enamel/dentin matrix gene set (ENAM, AMBN, AMELX, DSPP, MMP20, AMTN, ODAM), the Meredith et al. 2014 single-loss hypothesis and its critiques, dating of the lesions, and which specific frameshifts/stop codons are documented in Gallus gallus; which odontogenic regulatory genes (BMP4, SHH, PITX2, MSX1/2, BARX1, RUNX2, FGF8, LEF1, WNT/beta-catenin, EDA/EDAR) remain intact and functional in birds. (2) Experimental atavism precedents in chicken: talpid2 (C2CD3) mutant tooth germs (Harris et al. 2006), Kollar & Fisher 1980 and its replication controversy, Chen et al. 2000 Development on conserved odontogenic potential of avian mandibular epithelium, Mitsiadis et al. 2003 PNAS neural-crest recombination, Bhullar et al. beak-to-premaxilla reversion via FGF/WNT inhibition, Harris/Fallon work on scale-to-feather and tooth-germ induction; what exactly was recovered (rudimentary conical first-generation teeth vs mineralized enamel) and what failed. (3) Genetic control of axial elongation and tail termination in amniotes: GDF11, LIN28A/let-7, CDX1/2/4, HOX13 paralogs (HOXA13/HOXB13/HOXC13/HOXD13), WNT3A vestigial-tail, FGF8 gradient and retinoic acid (ALDH1A2/CYP26A1) in the neuromesodermal progenitor niche, TBXT/Brachyury including the Xia et al. 2024 Nature hominoid TBXT AluY tail-loss mechanism; the specific avian program that produces the pygostyle — caudal somite number, programmed cell death in the avian tail bud, Rashid et al. 2014 EvoDevo review, and comparison with Archaeopteryx/Caudipteryx caudal counts. (4) Comparative archosaur genomics and ontogeny: Alligator mississippiensis / Crocodylus porosus / Gavialis genomes as the intact-toolkit outgroup, polyphyodonty and the crocodilian dental lamina, conserved non-coding elements (CNEEs) lost or accelerated in the avian stem lineage, B10K/Bird 10,000 Genomes and other archosaur resources, and which developmental stages (HH stages vs crocodilian staging) are directly comparable. (5) In silico methodology for designing and scoring such edits: genomic language models (Evo 2, Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2) for variant-effect and regulatory-element scoring in non-human vertebrates and their validated limits; CRISPR/Cas9 and base/prime editing in chicken primordial germ cells (PGCs) and the state of germline-transgenic galliforme technology; enhancer and cis-regulatory element discovery in chicken (ATAC-seq/ChIP-seq atlases, ENCODE-like avian resources); protein structure prediction of amelogenin/enamelin/ameloblastin and the limits of folding intrinsically disordered enamel matrix proteins. (6) Ethical, welfare and regulatory framing for avian atavism research — institutional animal ethics review, the scientific-value critiques of the "dino-chicken" framing, and where the line sits between a legitimate evo-devo experiment and spectacle. Prioritize primary peer-reviewed literature with DOIs, note where claims are contested, and flag any claim that rests on a single non-replicated study.
claim: {"summary": "For the dental half of the question the verified literature converges on a clear answer: avian edentulism is a *two-tier* loss. The structural enamel/dentin matrix genes (AMEL/AMELX, ENAM, AMBN, DSPP, plus MMP20/AMTN in later work) are pseudogenized or physically rearranged in Gallus gallus and carry lesions shared across crown birds, which Meredith et al. 2014 read as a single loss of mineralized teeth in the ancestor of Neornithes (~116 Ma, a date later contested and revised downward to ~88-90 Ma); meanwhile the upstream odontogenic *regulatory* network (FGF8, PITX2, BARX1, PAX9, SHH, and inducible BMP/MSX) is intact, expressed in the chick mandible, and pharmacologically re-inducible, which is exactly why chick experiments recover tooth-germ-like and Shh-positive epithelial structures but never a mineralized enamel cap. The practical in-silico consequence is that re-accentuating archosaur dentition in Gallus cannot be done by regulatory de-repression alone: it requires transgenic reintroduction of functional matrix genes (the intact crocodilian/squamate orthologues being the natural donor set), and the specific editable lesions are documented (chicken AMEL 4-nt insertion in exon 2 causing a premature stop in exon 6; DSPP single-nucleotide deletion in the exon-2 remnant with exon-5 SDSSD repeats absent; a 406 bp deletion near the 3' end of ENAM exon 9 shared by five birds). One methodological warning is load-bearing: the 2008 claim that AMBN and ENAM were deleted outright was self-corrected in 2010 when chicken psi-ENAM was found off-synteny on chromosome Z, so every lesion coordinate must be re-derived against a current assembly (GRCg7b/bGalGal1) before it is used to design an edit. Nothing on the tail/axial-termination half of the question, on comparative archosaur genomics beyond ENAM, on in-silico scoring methodology (Evo 2/DNABERT-2, PGC editing, enhancer atlases, IDP folding), or on ethics/welfare survived verification in this pass - those sections are unanswered, not answered negatively.", "findings": [{"claim": "Mineralized teeth were lost once, in the common ancestor of modern birds (Neornithes), evidenced by inactivating mutations in enamel- and dentin-expressed genes shared across lineages of nearly all extant bird orders.", "confidence": "high", "vote": "3-0", "sources": ["https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1254390 (Meredith RW, Zhang G, Gilbert MTP, Jarvis ED, Springer MS, Science 346(6215):1254390, 2014, doi:10.1126/science.1254390, PMID 25504730)", "https://bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2148-13-20 (Meredith RW, Gatesy J, Springer MS, BMC Evol Biol 13:20, 2013, doi:10.1186/1471-2148-13-20)"], "evidence": "Verbatim abstract: 'We performed comparative genomic analyses representing lineages of nearly all extant bird orders and recovered shared, inactivating mutations within genes expressed in both the enamel and dentin of teeth of other vertebrate species, indicating that the common ancestor of modern birds lacked mineralized teeth.' Sample = the 48-genome Jarvis et al. 2014 avian phylogenomics dataset. The inference rests on present-but-lesioned orthologues carrying shared frameshifts/stops, NOT on gene absence, so it is immune to the avian 'false gene loss' artefact literature (Bornelov 2017; Hron 2018; Kim 2022 doi:10.1186/s13059-022-02765-0) that plagues GC-rich microchromosome calls in short-read bird assemblies. No published technical comment, eLetter or reanalysis arguing convergent within-crown loss was located in 12 years. THREE SCOPE LIMITS THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE CLAIM: (a) the authors hedge the phenotype themselves - 'tooth loss, OR AT LEAST the loss of enamel caps' - so single-loss is demonstrated for mineralized teeth/enamel, and total edentulism could have been staged; (b) the statement applies to CROWN birds only: among Mesozoic stem birds tooth loss was repeatedly and independently acquired (Confuciusornis, Gobipteryx, Archaeorhynchus, Schizooura; Brocklehurst & Field 2021, PMC7973866) and toothed ornithurines (Hesperornis, Ichthyornis) persisted to the end-Cretaceous; restating this loosely as 'birds lost teeth only once' IS an overreach; (c) the 2013 precursor paper's shared 406 bp ENAM exon-9 deletion strictly dates only to the Neognathae node, and the authors explicitly flagged that palaeognath sampling was needed - which the 2014 48-genome paper then supplied."}, {"claim": "The avian tooth-loss event is dated to ~116 Ma by Meredith et al., but that number is contested downstream and should be cited as an attribution rather than as settled fact.", "confidence": "medium", "vote": "2-1", "sources": ["https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1254390 (doi:10.1126/science.1254390)", "Brocklehurst N, Field DJ, iScience 2021, PMC7973866 (macroevolutionary dynamics of dentition in Mesozoic birds)"], "evidence": "Verbatim: 'We estimate that tooth loss, or at least the loss of enamel caps that provide the outer layer of mineralized teeth, occurred about 116 million years ago.' The dating is selection-relaxation / frameshift-accumulation dating on the pseudogenes placed on the modern-bird stem branch, not a fossil-calibrated node age - so the research prompt's phrase 'dating of the lesions' is loose but not a misread. CONTESTED: Brocklehurst & Field 2021 state directly 'Both of these are substantially younger than previous estimates (116 mya [Meredith et al., 2014a])' and report a median ~88-90 Ma for the transition to full edentulism. The 116 Ma figure is also contingent on the Jarvis et al. 2014 timetree, since revised (Prum et al. 2015; Stiller et al. 2024 Nature). Additionally, the widely-cited '~60 Myr' figure from Chen et al. 2000 is an outdated lower bound and should not be used; cite ~116 Ma (Meredith) or >=66 Ma (fossil record) with the ~88-90 Ma counter-estimate. The split vote reflects the contested number, not doubt about the attribution."}, {"claim": "Specific, editable lesions are documented in Gallus gallus for AMEL, DSPP and ENAM - these are the concrete coordinates any in-silico reversion design would target.", "confidence": "high", "vote": "3-0 (AMEL), 2-1 (DSPP), 3-0 (ENAM)", "sources": ["https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1471-2148-8-246 (Sire JY, Delgado SC, Girondot M, 'Hen's teeth with enamel cap: from dream to impossibility', BMC Evol Biol 8:246, 2008, doi:10.1186/1471-2148-8-246, PMC2542379, PMID 18775069)", "https://bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2148-13-20 (doi:10.1186/1471-2148-13-20, PMC3562159)", "https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/27/9/2078/1009898 (Al-Hashimi N, Lafont AG, Delgado S, Kawasaki K, Sire JY, Mol Biol Evol 27(9):2078-2094, 2010, doi:10.1093/molbev/msq098, PMID 20403965)"], "evidence": "AMEL (psi-AMEL): orthologue of crocodile AMEL exon 2 recovered ~38 kb upstream of ARHGAP6 exon 2 on chicken chr. 1, 68.8% nucleotide identity; a 4-nucleotide insertion in exon 2 (signal peptide) shifts the reading frame and yields a premature stop codon in exon 6. Caveats: the 4-nt insertion is causative but not the only lesion (further indels in exon 3 and both ends of exon 6; exons 1 and 4 never recovered); the finding is purely in silico from WASHUC2/galGal3 with no PCR/Sanger validation reported; the 'crocodile' comparator is GenBank AF095568 from Paleosuchus palpebrosus, NOT Alligator mississippiensis, and should be named by species. DSPP: only a putative exon 2 survives, ~5,800 bp from DMP1 in the SIBLING cluster on chr. 4, 54% identity to human DSPP exon 2 over a ~50 bp manually aligned window, carrying a single-nucleotide deletion that frameshifts; the characteristic SDSSD repeats of exon 5 are absent ('strongly suggests that this exon has been deleted'). The chicken SIBLING cluster is >12x more compact than human (40 kb vs 510 kb). Chromosome assignment still holds on a current assembly: ENSGALG00010002428 (IBSP/DMP1 locus) is on seq_region 4 at 45,249,489-45,255,379 in bGalGal1.mat.broiler.GRCg7b. Report the fragment length with the 54% figure and flag exon-5 'deletion' as an argument from absence, not an observed breakpoint. ENAM: 'All of the exon 9 sequences were characterized by frameshift mutations ... including a 406 bp deletion near the 3' end of the coding sequence of exon 9 that is shared by all five birds' - positions 3353-3758, taxa Gallus gallus, Meleagris gallopavo, Anas platyrhynchos, Melopsittacus undulatus, Taeniopygia guttata, alignment deposited as Additional file 1, so the lesion is literally checkable. A shared deletion sets a MINIMUM age for that lesion (Neognathae node); read dates as 'no later than'."}, {"claim": "The 2008 conclusion that AMBN and ENAM were physically deleted from the chicken genome was self-corrected in 2010: chicken psi-ENAM exists, located off-synteny on chromosome Z. This is a methodological warning, not just a historical footnote.", "confidence": "high", "vote": "3-0", "sources": ["https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1471-2148-8-246 (doi:10.1186/1471-2148-8-246)", "https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/27/9/2078/1009898 (doi:10.1093/molbev/msq098)"], "evidence": "Sire et al. 2008 searched two syntenically-defined candidate regions (14 kb and 700 kb, flanking IGJ/SULT1E1 on chr. 4) plus a genome-wide BLASTN using only the 54 bp exon-2 probes of crocodile AMBN and human ENAM: 'No positive hit was obtained in these regions. These genes have been likely deleted from the chicken genome as a consequence of intrachromosomal rearrangements'. Two inversions were identified in the IGJ-adjacent region. Al-Hashimi et al. 2010 - same senior author - then recovered chicken psi-ENAM by in silico search PLUS PCR, on chromosome Z downstream of LPL and upstream of NRG1/FUT10, i.e. entirely outside the mammal-synteny-guided search space, interpreted as a sauropsid-lineage translocation. Abstract: 'search for a pseudogene in the chicken genome ... we obtained and characterized ... the putative sequence of chicken ENAM pseudogene', concluding 'tooth loss in modern birds led to the invalidation of enamel genes'. TWO OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCES: (1) synteny-guided absence calls on 2008-era assemblies are unreliable - the enamelin locus persists as a degraded relic rather than being deleted outright; (2) AMBN remains the weakest link: Sire 2008 reports it absent, and 'recoverable AMBN remnants in birds' was NOT independently verified in this pass (several summaries of Meredith 2014 list the shared lesions as DSPP + ENAM/AMELX/AMTN/MMP20 without AMBN). Do not assert AMBN status without re-deriving it. All lesion coordinates should be re-mapped onto GRCg6a/GRCg7b/bGalGal1 before entering a methods section; the authors' own 2010 hedge 'putative' should also be preserved."}, {"claim": "The non-avian sauropsid outgroup retains a functional enamel-matrix toolkit: ENAM mRNA is transcribed and intact in crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus), lizard (Anolis carolinensis) and frog (Xenopus tropicalis) - but the verified evidence covers ONE gene, not the whole toolkit.", "confidence": "medium", "vote": "2-1", "sources": ["https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/27/9/2078/1009898 (doi:10.1093/molbev/msq098)", "Chen, Sire et al., EvoDevo 6:23, 2015, doi:10.1186/s13227-015-0024-4, PMC4587831", "Gasse et al. on amelotin in Alligator mississippiensis and Caiman crocodilus, PMC4373244", "https://bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2148-13-20 (doi:10.1186/1471-2148-13-20)"], "evidence": "Al-Hashimi 2010 recovered ENAM mRNA coding sequence for all three species (crocodile and lizard exon 4 to exon 10; frog full-length except the middle of the large exon 10), each a single isoform with intact signal peptide and conserved functional residues (3 putative phosphoserines, 3 N-glycosylation asparagines, 6 cysteines). Independently corroborated: Chen/Sire et al. 2015 EvoDevo demonstrated ENAM (with AMEL, AMBN, AMTN) actually expressed in Anolis carolinensis ameloblasts during amelogenesis - the first such demonstration in a non-mammal. OVERREACH FLAG: the phrase 'intact enamel-matrix toolkit' generalizes beyond the single gene this source establishes. AMELX/AMBN/AMTN/ODAM/MMP20/KLK4/DSPP intactness in these outgroups must be cited to Meredith et al. 2013 BMC Evol Biol 13:20, Sire et al. 2015 EvoDevo 6:23, and Gasse et al. on AMTN - not to Al-Hashimi 2010. Quoting the four retained regulators without the three absent ones would falsely imply an end-to-end intact cascade. Also note the research prompt miscites Chen et al. 2000 as 'Development'; it is PNAS."}, {"claim": "The latent chick odontogenic cascade is experimentally re-inducible: exogenous BMP restores Msx expression in chick mandibles and BMP+FGF promotes development of Sonic hedgehog-expressing epithelial structures - but what is recovered is Shh-positive epithelial structures/appendages of ambiguous tooth-vs-feather identity, never mineralized teeth.", "confidence": "high", "vote": "3-0", "sources": ["https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.160245097 (doi:10.1073/pnas.160245097, PMC27667)"], "evidence": "Verbatim: 'In chick mandibles, exogenous bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) induces Msx expression and together with fibroblast growth factor promotes the development of Sonic hedgehog expressing epithelial structures'; and 'Distinct epithelial appendages also were induced when chick mandibular epithelium was recombined with a tissue source of BMPs and fibroblast growth factors, chick skin mesenchyme'. It does not, however, demonstrate the formation in Aves of structures that can be called teeth.' No mineralization was reported; the induced structures 'were not typical tooth or feather germs, but exhibited some morphologic features consistent with both fates'. Method note: these were recombinant-protein beads and tissue recombination, not small-molecule pharmacology - 'pharmacologically inducible' is loose. Importantly, this is an ALL-AVIAN induction (chick epithelium + chick skin mesenchyme), which means early odontogenic signalling CAN be initiated in birds without heterologous mesenchyme, even though no tooth results."}, {"claim": "The Chen et al. 2000 proposal that loss of odontogenic Bmp4 expression is the specific cause of early arrest of avian tooth development is a single-node causal hypothesis that has never been independently confirmed, and a competing positional/epigenetic model exists.", "confidence": "medium", "vote": "2-1", "sources": ["https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.160245097 (doi:10.1073/pnas.160245097)", "Harris MP, Hasso SM, Ferguson MWJ, Fallon JF, Curr Biol 16(4):371-7, 2006, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2005.12.047, PMID 16488870", "Lainoff AJ et al., J Exp Zool B 324(3):255-69, 2015, doi:10.1002/jez.b.22594", "https://bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2148-13-20"], "evidence": "The paper's own wording is hedged - 'suggest that loss of odontogenic Bmp4 expression MAY BE responsible for the early arrest of tooth development in living birds' - and any downstream text must preserve 'proposed', not 'showed'. Of that recombination lineage, Kollar & Fisher 1980 is interpretively contested; Mitsiadis et al. 2003 is not.", "confidence": "medium", "vote": "2-1", "sources": ["https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982206000649 (Harris MP, Hasso SM, Ferguson MWJ, Fallon JF, 'The Development of Archosaurian First-Generation Teeth in a Chicken Mutant', Curr Biol 16:371-377, 2006, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2005.12.047)", "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1471-2148-8-246 (doi:10.1186/1471-2148-8-246)", "https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.160245097 (doi:10.1073/pnas.160245097)"], "evidence": "Verbatim from Harris et al. 2006: 'Although recombination studies have shown that the avian epidermis can respond to tooth-inductive cues from mouse or lizard oral mesenchyme and participate in tooth formation, attempts to initiate tooth development de novo in birds have failed.' 'Non-de-novo' applies to both; 'contested' applies only to Kollar & Fisher 1980. (2) The absolute 'only with heterologous mesenchyme' is too strong at the level of early odontogenic SIGNALLING: Chen et al. 2000 ran all-avian experiments (BMP/FGF induction of Shh-expressing buds; chick mandibular epithelium + chick skin mesenchyme) that initiated odontogenic signalling without heterologous tissue - yielding epithelial buds/appendages, never teeth. Only sections (1) and (2) of the six-part research question are actually answered by surviving claims. NOTHING survived on: section (3) axial elongation and tail termination (GDF11, LIN28A/let-7, CDX, HOX13 paralogs, WNT3A, FGF8/RA gradients, TBXT/Brachyury including Xia et al. 2024 Nature, pygostyle formation, avian tail-bud apoptosis, Rashid et al. 2014 EvoDevo, Archaeopteryx/Caudipteryx caudal counts); section (4) comparative archosaur genomics beyond the single ENAM gene (crocodilian genomes as outgroup, polyphyodonty and the crocodilian dental lamina, CNEEs lost/accelerated in the avian stem, B10K, HH-vs-crocodilian stage correspondence); section (5) in-silico methodology (Evo 2 / Nucleotide Transformer / DNABERT-2 variant-effect scoring and its validated limits in non-human vertebrates, CRISPR/base/prime editing in chicken PGCs, chicken ATAC-seq/ChIP-seq enhancer atlases, folding intrinsically disordered enamel-matrix proteins); section (6) ethics, welfare, regulatory framing and the 'dino-chicken' spectacle critique. Treat those as UNANSWERED, not as answered negatively - a second research pass is required before the tail half of the project has any evidentiary basis. SECOND: eleven claims were voted refuted, and inspection shows most failed on attribution/overreach wording rather than on being factually false - notably three Harris et al. 2006 talpid2 claims (archosaurian/crocodilian first-generation teeth, beta-catenin sufficiency, the lateral-signalling-centre model) and several Meredith 2013 lesion-inventory claims (AMEL exon-4 1-bp deletion; AMBN exon-3/6 frameshifts in Gallus). Do not cite those as verified, and do not cite them as disproved either; re-verify them directly against the primary texts if they are to be load-bearing. THIRD: assembly currency. Every coordinate above (chr. 1 AMEL/ARHGAP6, chr. 4 DSPP/SIBLING, chr. Z ENAM, ENAM exon 9 positions 3353-3758) derives from WASHUC2/galGal3 (2008) or 2011-2012 short-read assemblies. Only the chr. 4 SIBLING location was spot-checked against a modern assembly (GRCg7b, via Ensembl). Re-derive all lesions on GRCg7b/bGalGal1 before any edit design. FOURTH: several key homology calls are weak by modern standards - the DSPP exon-2 remnant is a ~50 bp manual alignment at 54% identity that GenBank's annotation pipeline did not call at all, and the AMBN/ENAM absence calls used 54 bp exon-2 probes. FIFTH: two single-study, non-replicated hypotheses must be flagged wherever used - the Chen et al. 2000 Bmp4-loss-causes-arrest hypothesis, and the Sire et al. 2008 'advanced predentin ceiling', which is a gene-content prediction never tested to failure. SIXTH: the 116 Ma date and the '60 Myr' figure are both time-sensitive and superseded; use ~116 Ma (Meredith) paired with ~88-90 Ma (Brocklehurst & Field 2021). SEVENTH: source mix is heavily weighted to one research group (Sire/Delgado/Girondot/Al-Hashimi) and one other (Meredith/Gatesy/Springer); independent corroboration exists but the field is small. EIGHTH: the research prompt itself contains two citation errors carried into the claims - Chen et al. 2000 is PNAS, not Development, and the 'crocodile' AMEL comparator is Paleosuchus palpebrosus, not Alligator.", "openQuestions": ["What is the genetic basis of avian tail termination and the pygostyle - is it gene loss (as with the enamel matrix) or purely regulatory/heterochronic? Nothing on GDF11, CDX, HOX13, TBXT, LIN28A/let-7, WNT3A, tail-bud apoptosis or caudal somite counts survived this pass, so it is currently unknown whether the two target traits (teeth and tail) have the same class of molecular lesion - which determines whether a single design strategy can address both.", "Is AMBN present as a recoverable relic in Gallus or genuinely deleted? Sire 2008 reports absence, the 2010 psi-ENAM discovery discredits the synteny-guided method that produced that absence call, and AMBN was the one gene not independently confirmed in the shared-lesion inventory. This must be settled against GRCg7b before an enamel-matrix restoration set can be specified.", "Given that atavism-by-reactivation is capped at predentin, what would a minimal transgenic complement actually be - which crocodilian orthologues (AMEL, AMBN, ENAM, AMTN, ODAM, MMP20, KLK4, DSPP) are jointly necessary and sufficient for enamel deposition, and is there any published knock-in evidence in any system that reintroducing matrix genes into an edentulous background restores mineralization?", "How well do genomic language models (Evo 2, Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2) actually perform on non-mammalian vertebrate regulatory and variant-effect scoring, and are they validated at all on avian genomes? This is the core methodological question for the project's in-silico scoring plan and no evidence on it was returned.", "Where does the institutional line sit between a defensible evo-devo experiment and the 'dino-chicken' spectacle framing, and what animal-ethics review path applies to germline-transgenic galliformes? Given the project's own CLAUDE.md routing of elevated-risk work to the biosafety committee, this needs an explicit answer before any wet-lab framing is written."]}
summary: For the dental half of the question the verified literature converges on a clear answer: avian edentulism is a two-tier loss. The structural enamel/dentin matrix genes (AMEL/AMELX, ENAM, AMBN, DSPP, plus MMP20/AMTN in later work) are pseudogenized or physically rearranged in Gallus gallus and carry lesions shared across crown birds, which Meredith et al. 2014 read as a single loss of mineralized teeth in the ancestor of Neornithes (~116 Ma, a date later contested and revised downward to ~88-90 Ma); meanwhile the upstream odontogenic regulatory network (FGF8, PITX2, BARX1, PAX9, SHH, and inducible BMP/MSX) is intact, expressed in the chick mandible, and re-inducible, which is exactly why chick experiments recover tooth-germ-like and Shh-positive epithelial structures but never a mineralized enamel cap. The practical in-silico consequence is that re-accentuating archosaur dentition in Gallus cannot be done by regulatory de-repression alone: it requires transgenic reintroduction of functional matrix genes (the intact crocodilian/squamate orthologues being the natural donor set), and the specific editable lesions are documented (chicken AMEL 4-nt insertion in exon 2 causing a premature stop in exon 6; DSPP single-nucleotide deletion in the exon-2 remnant with exon-5 SDSSD repeats absent; a 406 bp deletion near the 3' end of ENAM exon 9 shared by five birds). One methodological warning is load-bearing: the 2008 claim that AMBN and ENAM were deleted outright was self-corrected in 2010 when chicken psi-ENAM was found off-synteny on chromosome Z, so every lesion coordinate must be re-derived against a current assembly (GRCg7b/bGalGal1) before it is used to design an edit. Nothing on the tail/axial-termination half of the question, on comparative archosaur genomics beyond ENAM, on in-silico scoring methodology (Evo 2/DNABERT-2, PGC editing, enhancer atlases, IDP folding), or on ethics/welfare survived verification in this pass — those sections are unanswered, not answered negatively.

findings.claim: Mineralized teeth were lost once, in the common ancestor of modern birds (Neornithes), evidenced by inactivating mutations in enamel- and dentin-expressed genes shared across lineages of nearly all extant bird orders.
sources: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1254390 (Meredith RW, Zhang G, Gilbert MTP, Jarvis ED, Springer MS, Science 346(6215):1254390, 2014, doi:10.1126/science.1254390, PMID 25504730)
https://bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2148-13-20 (Meredith RW, Gatesy J, Springer MS, BMC Evol Biol 13:20, 2013, doi:10.1186/1471-2148-13-20)
findings.evidence: Verbatim abstract: 'We performed comparative genomic analyses representing lineages of nearly all extant bird orders and recovered shared, inactivating mutations within genes expressed in both the enamel and dentin of teeth of other vertebrate species, indicating that the common ancestor of modern birds lacked mineralized teeth.' Sample = the 48-genome Jarvis et al. 2014 avian phylogenomics dataset. The inference rests on present-but-lesioned orthologues carrying shared frameshifts/stops, NOT on gene absence, so it is immune to the avian 'false gene loss' artefact literature (Bornelov 2017; Hron 2018; Kim 2022 doi:10.1186/s13059-022-02765-0) that plagues GC-rich microchromosome calls in short-read bird assemblies. No published technical comment, eLetter or reanalysis arguing convergent within-crown loss was located in 12 years. THREE SCOPE LIMITS THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE CLAIM: (a) the authors hedge the phenotype themselves - 'tooth loss, OR AT LEAST the loss of enamel caps' - so single-loss is demonstrated for mineralized teeth/enamel, and total edentulism could have been staged; (b) the statement applies to CROWN birds only: among Mesozoic stem birds tooth loss was repeatedly and independently acquired (Confuciusornis, Gobipteryx, Archaeorhynchus, Schizooura; Brocklehurst & Field 2021, PMC7973866) and toothed ornithurines (Hesperornis, Ichthyornis) persisted to the end-Cretaceous; restating this loosely as 'birds lost teeth only once' IS an overreach; (c) the 2013 precursor paper's shared 406 bp ENAM exon-9 deletion strictly dates only to the Neognathae node, and the authors explicitly flagged that palaeognath sampling was needed - which the 2014 48-genome paper then supplied.

findings.claim: The avian tooth-loss event is dated to ~116 Ma by Meredith et al., but that number is contested downstream and should be cited as an attribution rather than as settled fact.
sources: Brocklehurst N, Field DJ, iScience 2021, PMC7973866 (macroevolutionary dynamics of dentition in Mesozoic birds)
findings.evidence: Verbatim: 'We estimate that tooth loss, or at least the loss of enamel caps that provide the outer layer of mineralized teeth, occurred about 116 million years ago.' The dating is selection-relaxation / frameshift-accumulation dating on the pseudogenes placed on the modern-bird stem branch, not a fossil-calibrated node age - so the research prompt's phrase 'dating of the lesions' is loose but not a misread. CONTESTED: Brocklehurst & Field 2021 state directly 'Both of these are substantially younger than previous estimates (116 mya [Meredith et al., 2014a])' and report a median ~88-90 Ma for the transition to full edentulism. The 116 Ma figure is also contingent on the Jarvis et al. 2014 timetree, since revised (Prum et al. 2015; Stiller et al. 2024 Nature). Additionally, the widely-cited '~60 Myr' figure from Chen et al. 2000 is an outdated lower bound and should not be used; cite ~116 Ma (Meredith) or >=66 Ma (fossil record) with the ~88-90 Ma counter-estimate. The split vote reflects the contested number, not doubt about the attribution.

findings.claim: Specific, editable lesions are documented in Gallus gallus for AMEL, DSPP and ENAM - these are the concrete coordinates any in-silico reversion design would target.
sources: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1471-2148-8-246 (Sire JY, Delgado SC, Girondot M, 'Hen's teeth with enamel cap: from dream to impossibility', BMC Evol Biol 8:246, 2008, doi:10.1186/1471-2148-8-246, PMC2542379, PMID 18775069)
https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/27/9/2078/1009898 (Al-Hashimi N, Lafont AG, Delgado S, Kawasaki K, Sire JY, Mol Biol Evol 27(9):2078-2094, 2010, doi:10.1093/molbev/msq098, PMID 20403965)
findings.evidence: AMEL (psi-AMEL): orthologue of crocodile AMEL exon 2 recovered ~38 kb upstream of ARHGAP6 exon 2 on chicken chr. 1, 68.8% nucleotide identity; a 4-nucleotide insertion in exon 2 (signal peptide) shifts the reading frame and yields a premature stop codon in exon 6. Caveats: the 4-nt insertion is causative but not the only lesion (further indels in exon 3 and both ends of exon 6; exons 1 and 4 never recovered); the finding is purely in silico from WASHUC2/galGal3 with no PCR/Sanger validation reported; the 'crocodile' comparator is GenBank AF095568 from Paleosuchus palpebrosus, NOT Alligator mississippiensis, and should be named by species. DSPP: only a putative exon 2 survives, ~5,800 bp from DMP1 in the SIBLING cluster on chr. 4, 54% identity to human DSPP exon 2 over a ~50 bp manually aligned window, carrying a single-nucleotide deletion that frameshifts; the characteristic SDSSD repeats of exon 5 are absent ('strongly suggests that this exon has been deleted'). The chicken SIBLING cluster is >12x more compact than human (40 kb vs 510 kb). Chromosome assignment still holds on a current assembly: ENSGALG00010002428 (IBSP/DMP1 locus) is on seq_region 4 at 45,249,489-45,255,379 in bGalGal1.mat.broiler.GRCg7b. Report the fragment length with the 54% figure and flag exon-5 'deletion' as an argument from absence, not an observed breakpoint. ENAM: 'All of the exon 9 sequences were characterized by frameshift mutations ... including a 406 bp deletion near the 3' end of the coding sequence of exon 9 that is shared by all five birds' - positions 3353-3758, taxa Gallus gallus, Meleagris gallopavo, Anas platyrhynchos, Melopsittacus undulatus, Taeniopygia guttata, alignment deposited as Additional file 1, so the lesion is literally checkable. A shared deletion sets a MINIMUM age for that lesion (Neognathae node); read dates as 'no later than'.

findings.claim: The 2008 conclusion that AMBN and ENAM were physically deleted from the chicken genome was self-corrected in 2010: chicken psi-ENAM exists, located off-synteny on chromosome Z. This is a methodological warning, not just a historical footnote.
findings.evidence: Sire et al. 2008 searched two syntenically-defined candidate regions (14 kb and 700 kb, flanking IGJ/SULT1E1 on chr. 4) plus a genome-wide BLASTN using only the 54 bp exon-2 probes of crocodile AMBN and human ENAM: 'No positive hit was obtained in these regions. These genes have been likely deleted from the chicken genome as a consequence of intrachromosomal rearrangements'. Two inversions were identified in the IGJ-adjacent region. Al-Hashimi et al. 2010 - same senior author - then recovered chicken psi-ENAM by in silico search PLUS PCR, on chromosome Z downstream of LPL and upstream of NRG1/FUT10, i.e. entirely outside the mammal-synteny-guided search space, interpreted as a sauropsid-lineage translocation. Abstract: 'search for a pseudogene in the chicken genome ... we obtained and characterized ... the putative sequence of chicken ENAM pseudogene', concluding 'tooth loss in modern birds led to the invalidation of enamel genes'. TWO OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCES: (1) synteny-guided absence calls on 2008-era assemblies are unreliable - the enamelin locus persists as a degraded relic rather than being deleted outright; (2) AMBN remains the weakest link: Sire 2008 reports it absent, and 'recoverable AMBN remnants in birds' was NOT independently verified in this pass (several summaries of Meredith 2014 list the shared lesions as DSPP + ENAM/AMELX/AMTN/MMP20 without AMBN). Do not assert AMBN status without re-deriving it. All lesion coordinates should be re-mapped onto GRCg6a/GRCg7b/bGalGal1 before entering a methods section; the authors' own 2010 hedge 'putative' should also be preserved.

findings.claim: The non-avian sauropsid outgroup retains a functional enamel-matrix toolkit: ENAM mRNA is transcribed and intact in crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus), lizard (Anolis carolinensis) and frog (Xenopus tropicalis) - but the verified evidence covers ONE gene, not the whole toolkit.
sources: Gasse et al. on amelotin in Alligator mississippiensis and Caiman crocodilus, PMC4373244
findings.evidence: Al-Hashimi 2010 recovered ENAM mRNA coding sequence for all three species (crocodile and lizard exon 4 to exon 10; frog full-length except the middle of the large exon 10), each a single isoform with intact signal peptide and conserved functional residues (3 putative phosphoserines, 3 N-glycosylation asparagines, 6 cysteines). Independently corroborated: Chen/Sire et al. 2015 EvoDevo demonstrated ENAM (with AMEL, AMBN, AMTN) actually expressed in Anolis carolinensis ameloblasts during amelogenesis - the first such demonstration in a non-mammal. OVERREACH FLAG: the phrase 'intact enamel-matrix toolkit' generalizes beyond the single gene this source establishes. AMELX/AMBN/AMTN/ODAM/MMP20/KLK4/DSPP intactness in these outgroups must be cited to Meredith et al. 2013 BMC Evol Biol 13:20, Sire et al. 2015 EvoDevo 6:23, and Gasse et al. on AMTN - not to Al-Hashimi 2010. Also note Xenopus tropicalis is an amphibian outgroup to Amniota, not a sauropsid, and its exon-10 interior was not fully sequenced, so 'functional' there rests on the recovered transcript plus conserved motifs rather than a complete ORF. For a donor-sequence design, the crocodilian orthologues are the phylogenetically appropriate source; verify each gene individually rather than assuming toolkit-wide intactness.

findings.claim: The upstream odontogenic regulatory network is NOT lost in birds: FGF8, PITX2, BARX1 and PAX9 are expressed in the chick mandible and demarcate a potential odontogenic region positionally equivalent to the mouse dental lamina, and a chick oral rudiment resembling the lamina stage of the mammalian molar germ does form. Avian tooth development is arrested early, not absent from the outset.
sources: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.160245097 (Chen Y, Zhang Y, Jiang TX, Barlow AJ, St Amand TR, Hu Y, Heaney S, Francis-West P, Chuong CM, Maas R, 'Conservation of early odontogenic signaling pathways in Aves', PNAS 97(18):10044-9, 2000, doi:10.1073/pnas.160245097, PMID 10954731, PMC27667)
Lainoff AJ, Moustakas-Verho JE, Hu D, Kallonen A, Marcucio RS, Hlusko LJ, J Exp Zool B 324(3):255-69, 2015, doi:10.1002/jez.b.22594, PMC4401653
Louryan S et al., J Morphol 283(2):207-18, 2021, doi:10.1002/jmor.21437
findings.evidence: Verbatim abstract: 'Similar to the mouse dental lamina, expression of Fgf8, Pitx2, Barx1, and Pax9 defines a potential chick odontogenic region' and 'in the chick oral cavity a rudiment forms that resembles the lamina stage of the mammalian molar tooth germ'. NOT a single-study claim: chick Barx1 craniofacial expression (Barlow et al.) and chick Fgf8 mandibular-epithelium expression are independently established; Lainoff 2015 reports conserved Pitx2, Pax9 and Barx1 expression in the independently edentulous turtle Trachemys scripta; Louryan 2021 reports SHH, BMP4, PITX2 and PAX9 in parrot beak epithelium and mesenchyme with high-level clusters in pseudotooth rudiments - a second bird family, 21 years later. TWO WORDING CORRECTIONS FOR ANY WRITE-UP: (1) downgrade 'homologous to the mouse dental lamina' to 'similar to / positionally equivalent to' - the paper says 'similar', and 'resembles', not formal homology; (2) MANDATORY PAIRING - the very next sentence of the same abstract states 'the expression of three molecules involved in tooth initiation, Bmp4, Msx1, and Msx2, are absent from the presumptive chick dental lamina'. Quoting the four retained regulators without the three absent ones would falsely imply an end-to-end intact cascade. (Note: the standalone claim about the three absent genes did not itself survive the verification vote (0-3), so cite it from the primary abstract directly rather than as an independently verified finding.) Also note the research prompt miscites Chen et al. 2000 as 'Development'; it is PNAS.

findings.claim: The latent chick odontogenic cascade is experimentally re-inducible: exogenous BMP restores Msx expression in chick mandibles and BMP+FGF promotes development of Sonic hedgehog-expressing epithelial structures - but what is recovered is Shh-positive epithelial structures/appendages of ambiguous tooth-vs-feather identity, never mineralized teeth.
findings.evidence: Verbatim: 'In chick mandibles, exogenous bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) induces Msx expression and together with fibroblast growth factor promotes the development of Sonic hedgehog expressing epithelial structures'; and 'Distinct epithelial appendages also were induced when chick mandibular epithelium was recombined with a tissue source of BMPs and fibroblast growth factors, chick skin mesenchyme'. The authors' own conclusion: 'although latent, the early signaling pathways involved in odontogenesis remain inducible in Aves'. CRITICAL SELF-LIMITATION in the full text (PMC27667): 'The present work suggests that in Aves early steps in the odontogenic pathway potentially exist in latent form. It does not, however, demonstrate the formation in Aves of structures that can be called teeth.' No mineralization was reported; the induced structures 'were not typical tooth or feather germs, but exhibited some morphologic features consistent with both fates'. Method note: these were recombinant-protein beads and tissue recombination, not small-molecule pharmacology - 'pharmacologically inducible' is loose. Importantly, this is an ALL-AVIAN induction (chick epithelium + chick skin mesenchyme), which means early odontogenic signalling CAN be initiated in birds without heterologous mesenchyme, even though no tooth results.

findings.claim: The Chen et al. 2000 proposal that loss of odontogenic Bmp4 expression is the specific cause of early arrest of avian tooth development is a single-node causal hypothesis that has never been independently confirmed, and a competing positional/epigenetic model exists.
sources: Harris MP, Hasso SM, Ferguson MWJ, Fallon JF, Curr Biol 16(4):371-7, 2006, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2005.12.047, PMID 16488870
Lainoff AJ et al., J Exp Zool B 324(3):255-69, 2015, doi:10.1002/jez.b.22594
findings.evidence: The paper's own wording is hedged - 'suggest that loss of odontogenic Bmp4 expression MAY BE responsible for the early arrest of tooth development in living birds' - and any downstream text must preserve 'proposed', not 'showed'. Three independent pressures on the hypothesis: (1) Lainoff et al. 2015 show the Bmp4 domain is also proximally limited in the TOOTHED opossum Monodelphis domestica and the Fgf8 domain distally limited in the TOOTHED alligator, concluding that 'a limited Bmp4 domain does not necessarily correlate with edentulism' and that odontogenesis initiation in non-murine amniotes is 'more complex than previously imagined'; (2) Harris et al. 2006 propose instead an epigenetic/positional model in which a lateral signalling centre is displaced relative to competent odontogenic mesenchyme, and recapitulate early talpid2 events via beta-catenin activation rather than by restoring Bmp4; (3) regulatory restoration of Bmp4 could not in any case restore enamel, given the shared inactivating frameshifts in the matrix genes predating the Neognathae split. The four-gene expression observation (finding above) is NOT contested; only this causal node is. NOTE: the related standalone claims about Harris et al. 2006 - that talpid2 teeth were 'archosaurian/crocodilian first-generation teeth', that beta-catenin activation in wild-type chicks reproduced the talpid2 early events, and the lateral-signalling-centre model - all FAILED the verification vote (0-3, 1-2, 0-3) and must be treated as unverified in this pass, even though they are referenced second-hand in the sources above.

findings.claim: The hard ceiling on avian dental atavism BY REACTIVATION: because the structural matrix genes are invalidated or gone, reactivated tooth germs can at most reach advanced predentin deposition (a step requiring mainly collagen matrix); an enamel cap is unachievable. This is a theoretical prediction from gene content, never experimentally demonstrated, and it does NOT exclude transgenic reintroduction.
findings.evidence: Verbatim: 'Eliciting well-developed, reptilian teeth (i.e. with enamel cap) in chicken will remain unachievable because all genes encoding the structural proteins crucial for enamel and dentine formation have been invalidated or have disappeared from the chicken genome. The odontogenic pathway remains inducible in chicken embryos because the genes required for tooth morphogenesis remain active in the chicken, involved in many developmental processes.' And: 'tooth germs that form with experimental reactivation of this pathway or in ta2 chicken mutants could develop until an advanced stage of predentin deposition because the process to this point requires mainly collagen matrix deposition.' FOUR QUALIFICATIONS THAT NARROW BUT DO NOT REFUTE IT, all directly relevant to an in-silico design: (a) SCOPE - the impossibility applies to atavism-by-reactivation of the ENDOGENOUS chicken program; it says nothing about, and does not exclude, transgenic/knock-in reintroduction of functional enamel-matrix genes. Presenting this as 'enamel in birds is impossible, full stop' is an overreach. (b) PREDICTION, NOT OBSERVATION - the predentin ceiling was never experimentally reached; the authors note 'the oldest ta2 died at stages E16' and explicitly leave open whether teeth with an enamel cap would have been obtained 'under different experimental conditions or if the chicken mutants had survived'. Flag as non-replicated at the experimental level. (c) GENE COVERAGE - Sire 2008 analysed only four genes (AMEL, DSPP, AMBN, ENAM); MMP20, AMTN and ODAM come from Meredith 2013/2014 and Springer et al. 2019 (ODAM, BMC Evol Biol, doi:10.1186/s12862-019-1359-6). Cite the lesion inventory from Meredith, not Sire. (d) Preserve Sire's two-mechanism distinction 'invalidated OR gone' (pseudogenization vs deletion); do not collapse it to 'pseudogenized'.

findings.claim: Pre-2006, no experiment had initiated tooth development de novo in an all-avian system; avian epidermis had been shown to participate in tooth formation only when recombined with heterologous (mouse or lizard) odontogenic mesenchyme. Of that recombination lineage, Kollar & Fisher 1980 is interpretively contested; Mitsiadis et al. 2003 is not.
sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982206000649 (Harris MP, Hasso SM, Ferguson MWJ, Fallon JF, 'The Development of Archosaurian First-Generation Teeth in a Chicken Mutant', Curr Biol 16:371-377, 2006, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2005.12.047)
findings.evidence: Verbatim from Harris et al. 2006: 'Although recombination studies have shown that the avian epidermis can respond to tooth-inductive cues from mouse or lizard oral mesenchyme and participate in tooth formation, attempts to initiate tooth development de novo in birds have failed.' Sire et al. 2008 independently concur that no experiment achieved differentiated avian teeth, and on Kollar & Fisher specifically: 'In 1980, Kollar and Fischer recombined chick dental epithelium with mouse mesenchyme and obtained teeth with an enamel cover, the famous "hen's teeth." ... However, a possible contamination of the mouse mesenchyme by mouse epithelium makes the interpretation uncertain.' TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) Do NOT lump Mitsiadis et al. 2003 with Kollar & Fisher under 'contested' - the same review treats Mitsiadis favourably ('showed that avian dental epithelium can still induce a nonavian developmental program in mouse neural crest-derived mesenchyme, resulting in tooth germ formation'). 'Non-de-novo' applies to both; 'contested' applies only to Kollar & Fisher 1980. (2) The absolute 'only with heterologous mesenchyme' is too strong at the level of early odontogenic SIGNALLING: Chen et al. 2000 ran all-avian experiments (BMP/FGF induction of Shh-expressing buds; chick mandibular epithelium + chick skin mesenchyme) that initiated odontogenic signalling without heterologous tissue - yielding epithelial buds/appendages, never teeth. Note also that the framing sentence is an introduction claim by the talpid2 authors themselves (partly self-serving), though corroborated by the independent Sire 2008 review; and the talpid2 result itself is a single mutant line (later tied to C2CD3, Chang et al. 2014) carrying its own replication caveat.

caveats: COVERAGE IS THE BIGGEST CAVEAT. Only sections (1) and (2) of the six-part research question are actually answered by surviving claims. NOTHING survived on: section (3) axial elongation and tail termination (GDF11, LIN28A/let-7, CDX, HOX13 paralogs, WNT3A, FGF8/RA gradients, TBXT/Brachyury including Xia et al. 2024 Nature, pygostyle formation, avian tail-bud apoptosis, Rashid et al. 2014 EvoDevo, Archaeopteryx/Caudipteryx caudal counts); section (4) comparative archosaur genomics beyond the single ENAM gene (crocodilian genomes as outgroup, polyphyodonty and the crocodilian dental lamina, CNEEs lost/accelerated in the avian stem, B10K, HH-vs-crocodilian stage correspondence); section (5) in-silico methodology (Evo 2 / Nucleotide Transformer / DNABERT-2 variant-effect scoring and its validated limits in non-human vertebrates, CRISPR/base/prime editing in chicken PGCs, chicken ATAC-seq/ChIP-seq enhancer atlases, folding intrinsically disordered enamel-matrix proteins); section (6) ethics, welfare, regulatory framing and the "dino-chicken" spectacle critique. Treat those as UNANSWERED, not as answered negatively — a second research pass is required before the tail half of the project has any evidentiary basis. SECOND: eleven claims were voted refuted, and inspection shows most failed on attribution/overreach wording rather than on being factually false — notably three Harris et al. 2006 talpid2 claims (archosaurian/crocodilian first-generation teeth, beta-catenin sufficiency, the lateral-signalling-centre model) and several Meredith 2013 lesion-inventory claims (AMEL exon-4 1-bp deletion; AMBN exon-3/6 frameshifts in Gallus). Do not cite those as verified, and do not cite them as disproved either; re-verify them directly against the primary texts if they are to be load-bearing. THIRD: assembly currency. Every coordinate above (chr. 1 AMEL/ARHGAP6, chr. 4 DSPP/SIBLING, chr. Z ENAM, ENAM exon 9 positions 3353-3758) derives from WASHUC2/galGal3 (2008) or 2011-2012 short-read assemblies. Only the chr. 4 SIBLING location was spot-checked against a modern assembly (GRCg7b, via Ensembl). Re-derive all lesions on GRCg7b/bGalGal1 before any edit design. FOURTH: several key homology calls are weak by modern standards — the DSPP exon-2 remnant is a ~50 bp manual alignment at 54% identity that GenBank's annotation pipeline did not call at all, and the AMBN/ENAM absence calls used 54 bp exon-2 probes. FIFTH: two single-study, non-replicated hypotheses must be flagged wherever used — the Chen et al. 2000 Bmp4-loss-causes-arrest hypothesis, and the Sire et al. 2008 "advanced predentin ceiling", which is a gene-content prediction never tested to failure. SIXTH: the 116 Ma date and the "60 Myr" figure are both time-sensitive and superseded; use ~116 Ma (Meredith) paired with ~88-90 Ma (Brocklehurst & Field 2021). SEVENTH: source mix is heavily weighted to one research group (Sire/Delgado/Girondot/Al-Hashimi) and one other (Meredith/Gatesy/Springer); independent corroboration exists but the field is small. EIGHTH: the research prompt itself contains two citation errors carried into the claims — Chen et al. 2000 is PNAS, not Development, and the "crocodile" AMEL comparator is Paleosuchus palpebrosus, not Alligator.
openQuestions: What is the genetic basis of avian tail termination and the pygostyle — is it gene loss (as with the enamel matrix) or purely regulatory/heterochronic? Nothing on GDF11, CDX, HOX13, TBXT, LIN28A/let-7, WNT3A, tail-bud apoptosis or caudal somite counts survived this pass, so it is currently unknown whether the two target traits (teeth and tail) have the same class of molecular lesion — which determines whether a single design strategy can address both.

Is AMBN present as a recoverable relic in Gallus or genuinely deleted? Sire 2008 reports absence, the 2010 psi-ENAM discovery discredits the synteny-guided method that produced that absence call, and AMBN was the one gene not independently confirmed in the shared-lesion inventory. This must be settled against GRCg7b before an enamel-matrix restoration set can be specified.

Given that atavism-by-reactivation is capped at predentin, what would a minimal transgenic complement actually be — which crocodilian orthologues (AMEL, AMBN, ENAM, AMTN, ODAM, MMP20, KLK4, DSPP) are jointly necessary and sufficient for enamel deposition, and is there any published knock-in evidence in any system that reintroducing matrix genes into an edentulous background restores mineralization?

How well do genomic language models (Evo 2, Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2) actually perform on non-mammalian vertebrate regulatory and variant-effect scoring, and are they validated at all on avian genomes? This is the core methodological question for the project's in-silico scoring plan and no evidence on it was returned.

Where does the institutional line sit between a defensible evo-devo experiment and the "dino-chicken" spectacle framing, and what animal-ethics review path applies to germline-transgenic galliformes? Given the project's own CLAUDE.md routing of elevated-risk work to the biosafety committee, this needs an explicit answer before any wet-lab framing is written.

refuted.claim: The inactivated gene set spans BOTH enamel-matrix and dentin-matrix genes (i.e. the lesions are not confined to the enamel module such as ENAM/AMELX/AMBN/MMP20 but extend to dentin, implicating DSPP-type genes), meaning the whole mineralized-tooth pathway — not just enamel — is pseudogenized in the avian stem lineage.

Inactivated copies of AMBN, AMEL and ENAM are present in divergent avian lineages (Galloanserae, Passeriformes, Psittaciformes), and all three genes carry shared frameshift mutations that predate the basal split in Neognathae — the phylogenetic evidence underpinning a single ancestral enamel-loss event in the avian stem rather than repeated independent losses.

AMEL carries an independent shared avian lesion — a one-base-pair deletion in exon 4 common to all five birds — providing a second locus corroborating a single ancestral inactivation; four of the five birds also retain a start codon shared with crocodylians.

Gallus gallus carries documented AMBN frameshift mutations in exons 3 and 6, while other birds bear lesions at different positions (Anas exons 6 and 8; Taeniopygia exon 6; a stop codon in Melopsittacus exon 8) — i.e. AMBN accumulated both shared and lineage-specific damage.

Teeth formed de novo in the talpid2 chicken mutant, and these were morphologically archosaurian — specifically crocodilian-type first-generation teeth — as established by direct comparison with Alligator tooth development. This is the central experimental atavism precedent for avian odontogenesis and rests on this single study's mutant line.

In vivo activation of beta-catenin in wild-type (non-mutant) chicken embryos reproduced the early developmental events observed in talpid2, identifying WNT/beta-catenin as a sufficient upstream trigger for the initial odontogenic program in birds without requiring the talpid2 mutation itself.

The authors propose that avian tooth loss arose from repositioning of a lateral signaling center relative to competent odontogenic mesenchyme, and that odontogenic developmental potential is retained in modern birds — implying the regulatory toolkit, not the mesenchymal competence, is the in silico edit target.

In the chicken (Gallus gallus) genome, the four structural dental matrix protein genes are either pseudogenized or absent: full-length AMEL is present but invalidated by a 4-nucleotide insertion causing a frameshift; only the N-terminal region of DSPP survives, invalidated by a single-nucleotide deletion causing a frameshift; and AMBN and ENAM are not found at all, having been lost via chromosomal rearrangement in a bird ancestor.

Because the structural enamel/dentin matrix genes are invalidated or deleted, no experimental manipulation (including reactivating odontogenesis in chicken) can yield a true enamel cap — the paper's central falsifiable negative claim about avian dental atavism.

The odontogenic regulatory/signalling gene network required for tooth morphogenesis remains intact and inducible in chicken embryos (unlike the structural matrix genes), because those genes are pleiotropically retained for other developmental processes — which is why tooth germs can be induced but not mineralized with enamel.

Three tooth-initiation genes — Bmp4, Msx1 and Msx2 — are NOT expressed in the presumptive chick dental lamina, identifying a specific node of pathway failure rather than wholesale loss of the odontogenic network.
